title: Words That Refuse to Move. Notes on the Language That Stays Home
body: Some words never emigrate. Every language keeps a small room of them. Words for the exact weight of a silence, for the way light falls at six in the evening, for a kind of tiredness that has no English name. You can carry a dictionary across an ocean and that room stays home. I have been sitting with one such word for years. It is not beautiful or ancient. It is a small everyday word, the kind used while doing something else, and it refuses to be translated because the thing it points at is built from a hundred tiny habits of a place. Learn the word and you have learned nothing. Live beside it for a season and you understand it without being able to say it. This is the quiet scandal of translation. The headlines cross, the recipes cross, the poems mostly cross, and the small connective tissue of a life does not. Two people can hold a whole conversation across languages and be perfectly understood, and then one of them uses the small home word and suddenly there is a distance no dictionary crosses. What interests me is why. It is not that the feeling is unique to one place; feelings are the most portable things we have. It is that the small words are load bearing. They hold up jokes, excuses, greetings, the tiny rituals of a market or a kitchen. A word like that is less like a stone you can carry and more like an arch. Move it and it stops being an arch. So the people who arrive in a new language live twice for a while. Once in the language they carry, once in the language around them, and the traffic between the two runs through gestures and guesses. It is exhausting and it is also, quietly, the fastest school of attention there is. You start noticing what people do with their voices, because the words themselves have gone on strike. In the end the room of untranslated words is not a wall. It is more like a window that shows you where a life is actually lived. In the small words, said while doing something else, to people who already know. Sit with your own language for a moment. Which small word of yours would never survive translation, and what is it really holding up?
